title: Cost of privacy in online learning
formal: In the hypothesis-stream model defined below, does every class with a finite nonprivate mistake bound also admit a private expected mistake bound independent of the horizon? Specifically, for every nonempty class \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal X}\) on a countable instance domain \(\mathcal X\), suppose there are a deterministic causal learner \(B\) and a finite \(M_H\) such that \(B\) makes at most \(M_H\) mistakes on every finite sequence realizable by \(H\). Must there then exist a finite \(C_H\) and a family of causal randomized learners \((A_T)_{T\ge2}\) such that for every integer \(T\ge2\), \(A_T\) is \((1,T^{-2})\)-differentially private and on every realizable sequence \(S=((x_t,y_t))_{t=1}^{T}\) satisfies \[\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf 1\{h_t(x_t)\ne y_t\}\right]\le C_H?\] The constant may depend on the class but not on \(T\) or the input sequence. This records the original source's main finite-mistake-versus-horizon-cost question under the later literature's explicit transcript and small-slack conventions; it does not assert the particular proposed square-root lower bound in its displayed candidate Theorem 1.
why: The question separates having an online learning algorithm from keeping its total lifetime error bounded while protecting every observed record. It tests whether the classical finite-mistake notion survives continual private publication of hypotheses. The negative resolution explains why qualitative sublinear private learnability can coexist with an unavoidable growing cumulative error.
status_note: The source’s main question has a negative answer in the explicitly recorded hypothesis-stream expected-mistake model: NeurIPS 2024 Theorem 4.3 applies at epsilon=1 and delta=T^-2 and forces logarithmically growing mistakes already for a fixed two-hypothesis class. The original candidate square-root formula was not matched to a theorem and is not claimed resolved. Publication, definitions, parameter scope and the 2025 follow-up were checked on 15 September 2026.

progress.text: The COLT open-problem contribution asks whether privacy introduces a growing cost in the finite-mistake model. Its prose question and candidate rate formulas must be distinguished.
Published NeurIPS 2024 Theorem 4.3 proves the logarithmic expected-mistake lower bound for any class containing a distinct non-complementary pair, under its explicit privacy-parameter conditions.

A later author manuscript gives a matching logarithmic horizon dependence for adaptive realizable private learning at fixed class complexity; it retains sublinear-learnability terminology rather than claiming a bounded lifetime error.

Checked the original question, the 2024 theorem and definitions, and the 2025 follow-up. The main horizon-independent expected-mistake implication under the recorded conventions is negatively resolved and archived. The stronger candidate square-root formula and fixed-success-probability variants are not attributed to that resolution.

sentences: A nonprivate online learner can sometimes make only finitely many mistakes over an arbitrarily long realizable sequence.
The historical question asks whether protecting the entire released hypothesis stream preserves that finite total error budget.
The review makes the output, expected-error criterion and small privacy-slack schedule explicit.
A published NeurIPS 2024 lower bound gives a negative answer already for a fixed class of two non-complementary hypotheses.
The question is archived with its interpretation recorded, while the source’s stronger proposed rate and different probability criteria are not presented as proved.

definitions: A hypothesis is a binary function on \(\mathcal X\). A sequence is realizable if one fixed \(h^{*}\in H\) satisfies \(y_t=h^{*}(x_t)\) for every round. At round \(t\), the learner releases a function \(h_t:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}\), based only on the previous labeled examples and private randomness; it is then given \((x_t,y_t)\) and incurs one mistake precisely if \(h_t(x_t)\ne y_t\). Output hypotheses may lie outside \(H\). All examples are selected before execution by an oblivious adversary that can know the learner but not its realized randomness. The privacy observer sees the whole sequence \((h_1,\ldots,h_T)\). For countable \(\mathcal X\), equip the space of binary functions with the product sigma-algebra; learner kernels and transcript events are measurable in this space. For every two labeled sequences \(S,S'\in(\mathcal X\times\{0,1\})^{T}\) differing at at most one position, and every measurable transcript event \(E\), require \[\Pr[A_T(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[A_T(S')\in E]+T^{-2}.\] Privacy applies on arbitrary inputs, including unrealizable inputs; only the mistake guarantee has the realizability promise. Both the example and its label belong to the protected record. The horizon is public and the learner may know it. Computational resources and hypothesis evaluation costs are unrestricted; this is a statistical existence question over causal probability kernels, not an efficient-learning problem. The nonprivate bound is deterministic and worst-case; the private bound is in expectation over the learner's randomness. A finite bound means one constant working over all horizons, not the trivial bound \(T\). Constant \(\varepsilon=1\) and the schedule \(\delta=T^{-2}\) make explicit a standard meaningful privacy regime used in the matching later lower bound. They are an editorial normalization of the original source's otherwise incomplete parameter statement.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication in Lean, or refute it by specifying a class with a finite nonprivate mistake bound and proving that every family of \((1,T^{-2})\)-private causal learners has unbounded worst-case expected mistakes as \(T\to\infty\). A refutation requires quantification over all such private learners, not merely over a subclass of algorithms. A sublinear but horizon-dependent upper bound does not prove the implication. The expected-mistake criterion is distinct from a bound that holds only with a fixed success probability.

source_formulation.text: Does ordinary finite-mistake online learnability imply private finite-mistake online learnability, or must privacy introduce a cost growing with the horizon?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

context_blocks.text: The classical mistake-bound model requires a finite total error budget for every realizable sequence, regardless of its length. Merely obtaining an error rate tending to zero is weaker: logarithmically many mistakes still violate a horizon-independent budget. This difference is central to interpreting the 2022 question and the later results.

The initial source writes the privacy inequality for an unspecified algorithm output and gives two proposed theorem statements with problematic quantifiers and privacy-parameter ranges. Its main prose question is clear about finite mistake bounds. This review uses the explicitly defined hypothesis-stream, expected-error model of the subsequent papers, records the small-slack normalization, and does not treat those flawed candidate rate formulas as an exact benchmark statement.

Theorem 4.3 of Li, Wang and Ye states that, for any fixed \(c\in(0,1)\), when \(\varepsilon\ge\log T/T^{1-c}\) and \(\delta\le\varepsilon/T\), every private online learner for a class containing two distinct non-complementary hypotheses has worst-case expected mistakes \(\Omega(\log T/\varepsilon)\), even against an oblivious adversary. Non-complementary means the hypotheses agree somewhere and disagree somewhere. The bound applies to \(\varepsilon=1,\delta=T^{-2}\) for all sufficiently large \(T\).

The two hypotheses on \(\mathcal X=\{0,1\}\) given by \(h_0(x)=0\) and \(h_1(x)=x\) form such a pair and have a nonprivate finite mistake bound of one. Consequently the later theorem provides a negative answer to the recorded universal implication with a fixed finite domain and a fixed two-element class. It does not require the hypothesis class to grow with \(T\).

The logarithmic lower bound does not rule out private online learnability defined by sublinear expected mistakes. The 2025 follow-up reports a logarithmic-in-horizon upper bound against adaptive adversaries for finite-Littlestone-dimension classes; with \(\delta=T^{-2}\), its additional \(\log(1/\delta)\) term has the same scale. Neither this result nor the 2024 lower bound proves the original draft’s suggested \(\sqrt T/\varepsilon\) cost.
